speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In a fair and just society, we recognise that people do not get to choose where or when they will be born; that people do not get to choose their parents; that children do not get to choose their genetic background.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And today, I am speaking about the challenges faced by children with rare diseases.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Each of us inherits half our genes from our father, one half from our mother.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Sometimes, a gene is inherited which does not work the way it is expected to.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If there is a copy from the other parent which is working all right, the child may still be fine.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But in some cases, a child is doubly unlucky and inherits two copies of a flawed gene.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Not much published literature is available on the Singapore experience, but a 2006 paper in the Annals of the Academy of Medicine (Singapore) reported a 13-year experience at the Singapore General Hospital reference laboratory.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, even with better technology, better testing and better awareness, the number would still be small.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: However, even if rare, they can be devastating for a child and worrying for the parents.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And even if the disease is so rare that the odds of getting it are 0.001%, for the child who gets the disease, the impact is 100%.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Pompe disease is caused by the lack of an enzyme called acid alpha-glucosidase.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is a rare disease; some estimate it affects between one in 40,000 or as few as one in 138,000.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It affects the muscles, including the muscles of the heart.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, children with Pompe disease have weak hearts, get heart failure and can have difficulty moving or breathing.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Without treatment, the classic severe early-onset type of Pompe disease is devastating.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The median age at death for children with the severe form of the disease is nine months.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Deputy Speaker, Gaucher disease is another rare disease, caused by the lack of an enzyme in the body.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In children with Gaucher disease, the liver and spleen will swell and swell.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The brain and other organs can be affected, too.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In the more serious cases, the children can die before the age of two years.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There are treatments for Gaucher disease, which work by replacing the missing enzyme in the body.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But again, the treatment can be very expensive, with some estimate at over $20,000 a month.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Another rare disease is bile acid synthesis disorder and it is very rare, even among rare diseases.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Fewer than 50 reported cases around the world, in the international medical literature.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But we also have a little boy in Singapore who, unfortunately, has this rare disease.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There is a drug available, called cholic acid.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But the cost was estimated at over $25,000 per month.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Even with parallel imports from other markets, the drug cost was reported as about $5,000 per month.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Deputy Speaker, what these rare genetic diseases, and similar diseases, have in common are: (a) the condition is rare; (b) the impact is catastrophic; and (c) the need for treatment is not elective.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Indeed, treatment is necessary for the child to continue living a normal life.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Or in some cases, to carry on continue living.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Another recurring theme is that the drugs are very expensive and can be very hard to get hold of.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, there are no economies of scale for the producer.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The costs of research and development can be very high.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There are administrative overheads with registering such “orphan drugs” in Singapore, as they call it, and there is little commercial interest in developing such drugs or making them widely available at a good price even if development is successful by the drug company.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The affected families may be small in number.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But we must not leave behind any Singaporean child.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And over the past decade, since the mid-2000s, it is clear that our Government thinking has shifted towards a more inclusive society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our social policies today include the Workfare Income Supplement, ComCare, Edusave Bursaries and many, many more.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Part of a progressive fiscal system where the fruits of progress are shared, especially with the less well-off and the less fortunate.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And we can see that the Ministry of Health (MOH) has shifted, too, over the years, as part of what some have called an evolving New Way Forward.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: MediFund was set up in 1993 as an endowment fund to help needy Singaporeans with medical bills.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is a social policy to help Singaporeans from all walks of life, in case of serious illness with catastrophic medical bills, serious illness.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Importantly, MediShield Life helps, regardless of whether one is very old or whether one has a pre-existing condition from birth.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There is also the Medication Assistance Fund (MAF) and MAF Plus to help patients access new medications which may be beyond their means but which could still benefit the patients.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Deputy Speaker, at the same time, no policy is perfect.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is a commonsense move and it is not a radical policy shift either.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In fact, it is very much aligned with the deeper philosophy that already underpins our current social and healthcare policies.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, let us look at risk pooling.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: MediShield Life and other policies recognised the role of pooling risk, of sharing risk within the cohort or the population.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because the condition is genetic, because it is inborn, there is no direct moral hazard from providing that extra coverage and support.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Furthermore, Deputy Speaker, the private sector insurance market cannot adequately address this issue.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And insurance companies, being profit maximisers, will act in accordance with their business interests and this means that insurers will cherry pick who they want to cover.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In particular, would we want a child with rare diseases to be supported, if that child were our son or our daughter?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Would we want the parents to have peace of mind, if the parents were our friends or family?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And especially when doing so is a natural progression and harmonisation of existing policies and existing policy philosophy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I said back then, “We do not choose our parents or when we will be born.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we must always be a fair and just society.” Indeed, Mr Deputy Speaker, we do not choose our parents.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We do not choose the genes we inherit from our parents.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so, we must continue to be a fair and just society – for healthy children, as well as children born with rare diseases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As a parent, I empathise with the challenges all parents encounter and the daily struggles we have to go through to care for our children.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Parents of children with rare diseases will undoubtedly face even greater challenges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I agree with Dr Tan that as a caring and inclusive society, we should pool our resources together and do what we can to support these families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Singaporeans have access to good quality subsidised healthcare at public hospitals, specialist outpatient clinics and polyclinics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Many of our subsidies are means-tested to provide more support for Singaporeans with lower incomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And this is part of our progressive social policy and safety net.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On top of Government subsidies, we have MediShield Life, which provides universal protection for all Singaporeans against large hospital bills and costly outpatient treatments through risk-pooling.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government provides means-tested subsidies to help Singaporeans pay for their MediShield Life premiums.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We also offer financial assistance for low-income Singaporeans through Additional Premium Support to ensure that no Singaporean will lose coverage because he is unable to afford his premiums.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, MediShield Life, as Dr Tan pointed out, is not just an insurance scheme, it is a social policy which reflects our values as a community to build a fair and just society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For needy families who still require financial assistance after Government subsidies and MediShield Life payouts, and using their MediSave and other personal savings, we have MediFund as a further safety net to ensure that no Singaporeans will be denied access to appropriate care due to their financial situation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These social policies and assistance schemes are possible because we have grown our economy over the years, we have generated the required resources and we have managed our system efficiently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Now, as we face an ageing population in Singapore, we must continue to pay careful attention to these important areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: With these policies in place, the vast majority of Singaporeans are able to pay for their medical treatments and drugs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Yet, as Dr Tan has pointed out, even the best policies cannot address all circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There will be rare diseases where treatments and drugs are very expensive, and our insurance schemes, our subsidies will not provide adequate coverage for the patients and their families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When we encounter such cases, our public healthcare institutions will do their best to help.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There was a recent example in one of our public hospitals – a patient by the name of Emily who was diagnosed with Pompe disease since she was a teenager.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Emily needs to visit Changi General Hospital (CGH) every fortnight to receive an infusion of her missing enzymes, which is a costly drug.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Emily's father is a technician and her mother a homemaker and she has a sister who is still schooling.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Financially, it is very challenging for the family.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: CGH reached out to the family and brought in other parties to help.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Emily received subsidies for consultations and investigations, and the hospital helped her apply for funding under the Medication Assistance Fund.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These covered a significant proportion of the infusion cost.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The hospital also engaged a pharmaceutical company, which kindly agreed to extend financial assistance to further defray the cost of the medication she needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I am heartened to know that Emily is coping well with her treatment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Another example is Chloe, a little girl with the same condition as Emily.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Like Emily, she needs to visit the hospital regularly to receive the infusion of enzymes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is another example of how multiple parties have come together to support the family.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Government subsidies were provided for her treatment, the family’s insurance policy covered the post-subsidy costs of Chloe’s inpatient treatment, and additional Government and hospital assistance supported the other aspects of her treatment, such as mobility devices and consumables.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Dr Tan also mentioned in his speech a young boy, the name of this boy is Christopher, who was diagnosed with a rare disease called bile acid synthesis disorder.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The public hospital which is looking after Christopher is KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital (KKH) and they are working with the manufacturer to try and bring down the cost of the drugs for the family.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I have also asked my colleagues in MOH and KKH to assist Christopher’s family and find a way to help them to reduce their out-of-pocket expenses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is not an easy challenge to solve because many of the cases have unique circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: What is clear is that, as a caring and inclusive society, we must do our best to find practical ways to help our fellow Singaporeans who are in these difficult situations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This requires a collective effort from the public, private and people sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: By harnessing the collective giving from all parts of our community, we can help these families and create opportunities to encourage philanthropy and build a more caring society.
